blocks.x: Instruments, transfer restrictions and custody decide success — not chain choice.
Tokenization is a legal program with a cryptographic runtime. Permissioned transfer controls (whitelists, locks) are the compliance heart of every token.
Qualified custody and transfer-agent integration separate pilots from products.
Lifecycle automation (coupons, redemptions) is where operations cost actually falls.
Where this goes wrong in practice
Where it breaks in practice: technology-first scoping: a chain chosen before the trust question is answered, producing a ledger everyone must trust but nobody needs.

The strongest counter-case, stated fairly: the trust-first thesis can end in a ledger nobody joins. Shared truth only pays when every participant's incentives point the same way — verify that before the protocol choice.

In delivery, this thesis becomes a specific discipline: the trust layer is engineered, not asserted: signed events, permissioned consensus, and a provenance graph every participant can verify. Every program in the Blockchain & Digital Trust domain carries the same obligations — a signed baseline, named gate criteria, and evidence generated by running the system rather than preparing for a meeting.
Talk to the team that runs tokenization is a legal program with a cryptographic runtime in production — the briefing is technical by design, and the first one costs nothing but the hour.
